variants.name: C11 generic selection table
variants.implementation_notes: C has neither templates nor overloading, so the descriptor cannot be a class: the type-to-behaviour mapping is a table of macros and functions that must be kept in step by naming convention, and C11's generic selection picks a branch from the type of a controlling expression (6.5.1.1) - the mechanism tgmath.h adopted for type-generic math. The association list is closed, and without a default association an unlisted type is a compile error, which is the closest C gets to a compile-time 'unsupported type' diagnostic; but a type's properties (limits, precision, end-of-sequence value) cannot be inspected at all, so they must be named per type by convention next to the operations. Switch to a tagged union or an explicit function-pointer table once the set of types becomes open or the choice must be made at runtime.
pitfalls: The controlling expression is converted before matching (arrays decay to pointers, top-level qualifiers are dropped), so the association list must name the post-conversion type or the argument falls through to the default association.

No two associations may name compatible types and there is at most one default: adding a type to a family silently means editing the table, and a forgotten type breaks the build for every caller of the macro rather than at the definition site.
Type names in associations must be complete, non-variably-modified object types, so structures declared behind a forward declaration cannot be described until the type is complete.

variants.name: Pre-C11 type-suffixed function families
variants.idiom_name: per-type function families plus suffix macros or compiler builtins
variants.implementation_notes: Without _Generic the same mapping is built from per-type function families with a naming convention (len_int, len_double, len_cstr) and macros that select one entry point, either explicitly at the call site or through compiler builtins - C99's tgmath.h itself was implemented this way per compiler, which is why C11 added generic selection. Choose this form when the toolchain is C99 or older, and note its one advantage: because the family is named explicitly, the description can be chosen per call site instead of being fixed by the static type of the argument.
pitfalls: Nothing links the family to the type: passing the wrong suffix compiles (int and double variants have different signatures but a pointer argument fits several families) and fails only at runtime.
Macro-based selection cannot see through typedefs or qualifiers the way _Generic's conversion rules do, so a typedef'd parameter needs its own entry or an explicit suffix at every call site.
